<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>Background
 The homologous recombination (HR) repair pathway for DNA damage, particularly the <jats:italic>BRCA1</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>BRCA2</jats:italic> genes, has become a target for cancer therapy, with poly ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors showing significant outcomes in treating germline <jats:italic>BRCA1/2</jats:italic> (g<jats:italic>BRCA1/2</jats:italic>) mutated breast cancer. Recent studies suggest that some patients with somatic <jats:italic>BRCA1/2</jats:italic> (s<jats:italic>BRCA1/2</jats:italic>) mutation or mutations in HR-related genes other than <jats:italic>BRCA1/2</jats:italic> may benefit from PARP inhibitors as well, particularly those with <jats:italic>PALB2</jats:italic> mutations. The current analysis aims to evaluate the prevalence of genetic alterations specific to <jats:italic>BRCA1</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>BRCA2</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>PALB2</jats:italic> in a large cohort of Taiwanese breast cancer patients through tumor-targeted sequencing.
Methods
 A total of 924 consecutive assays from 879 Taiwanese breast cancer patients underwent tumor-targeted sequencing (Thermo Fisher Oncomine Comprehensive Assay v3). We evaluated <jats:italic>BRCA1</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>BRCA2</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>PALB2</jats:italic> mutational profiles, with variants annotated and curated by the ClinVAR, the Oncomine™ Knowledgebase Reporter, and the OncoKB™.
Results
 Among the 879 patients analyzed (924 assays), 130 had positive mutations in <jats:italic>BRCA1</jats:italic> (3.1%), <jats:italic>BRCA2</jats:italic> (8.6%), and <jats:italic>PALB2</jats:italic> (5.2%), with a total of 14.8% having genetic alterations. Co-occurrence was noted between <jats:italic>BRCA1/BRCA2</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>BRCA1/PALB2</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>BRCA2/PALB2</jats:italic> mutations. In <jats:italic>BRCA1</jats:italic>-mutated assays, only p.K654fs was observed in three patients, while other variants were observed no more than twice. For <jats:italic>BRCA2</jats:italic>, p.N372H was the most common (26 patients), followed by p.S2186fs, p.V2466A, and p.X159_splice (5 times each). For <jats:italic>PALB2</jats:italic>, p.I887fs was the most common mutation (30 patients). This study identified 176 amino acid changes; 60.2% (106) were not documented in either ClinVAR or the the Oncomine™ Knowledgebase Reporter. Using the OncoKB™ for annotation, 171 (97.2%) were found to have clinical implications.
Conclusion
 Our study depicted the mutational patterns of <jats:italic>BRCA1</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>BRCA2</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>PALB2</jats:italic> in Taiwanese breast cancer patients through tumor-only sequencing. This highlights the growing importance of <jats:italic>BRCA1/2</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>PALB2</jats:italic> alterations in breast cancer susceptibility risk and the treatment of index patients. We also emphasized the need to meticulously annotate variants in cancer-driver genes as well as actionable mutations across multiple databases.</jats:p>
title: Prevalence of BRCA1, BRCA2, and PALB2 genomic alterations among 924 Taiwanese breast cancer assays with tumor-only targeted sequencing: extended data analysis from the VGH-TAYLOR study
